longo.nar: There is a company that holds a file on you. You never signed up for it, you cannot delete it, and you are not its customer. You are its inventory.
Three of them, actually. Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Between them they hold a file on nearly every adult in the country.
That file decides whether you get an apartment, what you pay for insurance in many states, and in some cases whether you get the job at all.
And yet nobody in that transaction is buying anything from you. The lender is the customer. The landlord is the customer. You are the thing being sold.

Experian reported trailing revenue of about seven point five two billion dollars in its first half of fiscal twenty twenty-six. Equifax guided to between six point six six and six point seven eight billion for the year.
Together with TransUnion, that is well over fifteen billion dollars a year, built almost entirely on information that people hand over without ever deciding to.
This video follows that money. Not how to raise your score — there are ten thousand videos on that. How the business underneath it actually works.

itens: Why the score is a separate business
longo.nar: Four parts: what is actually in the file, who buys it and why, why the score itself is a completely separate business, and what all of it costs you in real money.

longo.preco: this is not a scam story
longo.nar: One thing up front. This is not a story about a scam. Everything here is legal, disclosed, and regulated. That is exactly what makes it worth understanding.
The system works. It is efficient, it prices risk well, and it lets strangers lend to strangers. It simply was not designed with you as the beneficiary.
So let us start with the thing itself. What is actually written in your file?
Four categories. Identifying information, the accounts you hold, your payment behaviour on each, and a log of everyone who has requested the file.
The identity section is thinner than people expect. Name, current and former addresses, date of birth, and in most cases a social security number.
The accounts section is the bulk of it. Every credit card, loan, mortgage and line of credit, with its limit, balance and age.
Payment history is recorded month by month, for years. Not a summary — a grid, with a mark for every billing cycle you have ever had.
The grid matters because lenders are not really pricing whether you paid. They are pricing the pattern. A single miss four years ago reads very differently from three misses last spring.
The last section is the inquiry log: every company that pulled your file, and when. It is the part almost nobody reads, and it quietly reveals a lot about the business.
Now the part that surprises people. Several things you would expect to be in the file simply are not.
Your income is not in there. Neither are your savings, your job title, or anything you own outright. The file describes your debt, not your wealth.
Which produces an odd result. A person who has never borrowed, who pays cash and owns their home, can look almost invisible to the system.
That is not a flaw in the data. It is the design. The file exists to describe how you handle borrowed money, and nothing else.
Which brings us to the question that actually explains the revenue. Who is asking to see it?
The obvious buyer is the lender. A bank deciding on a card or a mortgage pulls the file, and pays for it. That is the business everyone assumes.
But lending is nowhere near the whole story, and the other buyers are where the interesting money is.
Landlords screening tenants. Insurers in many states. Employers running background checks. Utility companies. And debt collectors deciding who is worth pursuing.
The insurance one catches people off guard. In many states an insurer may use a credit-based score to help set your premium, on the argument that it predicts claims.
Which means a thin or damaged file can raise what you pay for car insurance, in a transaction that has nothing to do with borrowing at all.
Then there is the part that explains the mailbox. Bureaus sell lists, in bulk, before anyone has applied for anything.
A card issuer describes the customer it wants — a score band, an age range, a region. The bureau returns a list of people who match, and the issuer mails them.
That is why offers arrive addressed to you for products you never looked at. You were not targeted by accident. You were selected, and someone paid for the selection.
You can opt out of that specific use. The mechanism exists, it is free, and almost nobody uses it, because almost nobody knows the list exists.
And there is one more buyer, the one that closes the loop. They sell it back to you.
Credit monitoring, score tracking, identity alerts — subscription products, sold to the person the file is about, describing the file they already own.

You are legally entitled to your reports for free. The paid product sells convenience and alerts on top of information you can already get. But it cannot sell you the number, and that is the part worth understanding: where does the score actually come from?
Here is where most explanations go wrong. The file and the score are two different products, made by two different kinds of company.
longo.cap: The score is a different business

longo.nar: The bureau holds the data. That is one business: collect, store, verify, sell access.
The score is a model that turns that data into a number. Building that model is a separate business, with a separate owner, taking a separate cut.
The best known of those models comes from Fair Isaac. The bureaus license the formula, run your data through it, and resell the result along with the file.
Which means a single credit pull often pays two companies. One for the data, one for the number calculated from it.
That arrangement works right up until one side decides it would rather have the whole margin.
Which is roughly what happened. Fair Isaac moved to sell scores directly to mortgage lenders and resellers, going around the bureaus.
Equifax responded by pushing VantageScore more aggressively into mortgage — a competing model, built by the bureaus themselves.
Stripped of the press releases, that is a fight over who keeps the margin on a number describing you, in which you have no seat and no vote.
It also explains something confusing: there is no single score. Different models, different bureaus, different versions, all producing different numbers about the same person.

So when an app shows you a score, the honest question is which model, which bureau, and which version — because a lender may be looking at a different one entirely. And if the number can differ, so can the record underneath it. Which leaves one question:
You have a legal right to dispute anything in the file, and disputes genuinely do get things removed. But the shape of the process tells you something.
longo.cap: Why disputes work the way they do

longo.nar: The burden starts with you. You must find the error, in a file you did not compile, describing accounts opened by companies you may not remember.
The bureau then asks the company that reported the item whether it is correct. That company is the bureau's customer.
Which is why a dispute is frequently returned as confirmed. The check is real, but it is a check with the party that supplied the information in the first place.
Volume explains most of the rest. With files on nearly every adult, disputes arrive in enormous numbers, and the process is built to run at that scale.
So it is heavily automated. That is not malice; it is arithmetic. But automation is why a nuanced dispute and a simple one can come back looking the same.
The practical consequence is that specific, documented disputes do far better than general ones. Name the account, the date, the exact field, and attach proof.
Medical debt has become its own category, because it behaves differently from borrowing: it arrives without a decision, often without a price known in advance.
The rules on how medical debt appears have moved repeatedly in recent years. If you have any on file, it is worth checking what currently applies rather than what applied last time you looked.
The same is true of old negative items. Most fall off after a defined period, and items that should have aged off sometimes do not, on their own.
Which leaves the question that actually matters to your money. What does all of this cost you?
The clearest place to see it is a mortgage, because the loan is large and it runs for decades.
longo.cap: What it costs you in real money

longo.nar: Between the top score band and a lower one, the rate difference on the same loan is routinely more than a full percentage point.
On a thirty-year loan, a difference of one point can mean tens of thousands of dollars in additional interest, for the identical house and identical borrower.
Same person, same income, same job. The only variable is the file — and the file mostly measures how long you have been borrowing and how consistently you repaid.
Then there are the smaller charges, which are easier to ignore and land more often.
Insurance premiums in many states. Larger rental deposits. Deposits for phone and utility service. And the rate on any card you carry a balance on.
Each one is small enough to shrug at. The pattern is not: the same file makes the same person more expensive in a dozen unrelated places at once.
The reverse compounds as well, which is the genuinely encouraging part of this.
Improving the file does not just lower one rate. It lowers several prices at once, in transactions you were not thinking about when you made the change.
And the mechanism is deliberately boring: pay on time, keep balances well below limits, and let accounts age. There is no clever move, because the model is mostly measuring time.

That is the honest answer to how you improve it, and it is why the improvement videos all end up saying roughly the same thing. But boring is not the same as nothing. There are four things worth doing, and every one of them is free:
Four things that cost nothing: pull all three reports, opt out of prescreened offers, freeze the file, and dispute specific errors with documentation.
Pull all three, not one. The bureaus receive different data from different companies, and an error often exists on only one of them.
The freeze is the strongest tool most people never use. It blocks new accounts from being opened against your file until you lift it.
It is free by law, reversible in minutes, and it does not affect your score or your existing accounts at all.
The trade-off is one extra step whenever you genuinely apply for something. For most people that is a few minutes a year against a permanent reduction in exposure.
Opting out of prescreened offers stops your name being sold into those bulk marketing lists. It is one form, and it does not affect anything else.
It is also the one place in this entire system where you can directly remove yourself from a revenue stream, which makes it worth doing on principle alone.
And one thing worth being blunt about: what is usually not worth paying for.
Credit repair companies mostly perform disputes you can file yourself, at no cost, using the same process and the same evidence.
And no service can remove an accurate item. If a claim to do so is made, that alone tells you what kind of company it is.
Everything else is just time. Which is unsatisfying, and also true. So it is worth stepping back and asking what this file really is:
Step back from the mechanics and there is a pattern worth naming, because it is not unique to credit.
A record is compiled about you without your involvement, sold to institutions that make decisions about you, and then sold back to you as a subscription.
That shape shows up in tenant screening, in employment background checks, in insurance rating. Credit is simply the oldest and most refined version of it.
The useful reaction is not outrage. Systems like this exist because the alternative — lending only to people you personally know — was far worse and far smaller.
The useful reaction is knowing you are inside a market you did not enter, and using the few levers that market gives you.

itens: You are the product, not the client
The file measures debt, not wealth
Time does most of the work
longo.nar: Three things to carry: you are the product and not the client. The file measures debt, not wealth. And time does most of the work, in both directions.
The first one changes how you read every offer that arrives unsolicited: someone paid to put your name on that list.
The second explains why paying cash for everything can leave you looking invisible, and why that is not a compliment.
If this was useful, tell me in the comments which institution you want taken apart next. The most requested one gets made first.
And if you have ever had something removed from your file, say what actually worked. Specifics help more people than general advice does.
Thanks for watching to the end. See you in the next one, here on Next Level Money.

short.nar: Three companies hold a file on you. You never signed up, you cannot delete it, and you are not their customer.
Your income is not in it. Neither are your savings. It describes how you handle borrowed money, and nothing else.
And the score is a separate business. One pull often pays two companies: one for the data, one for the number.
Freezing the file and opting out of prescreened offers are both free, and almost nobody does either.
So do one thing today. Freeze your file at all three bureaus, not one. It is free by law, it takes minutes, and it never touches your score.
